Welcome to my portfolio for MUSA 5080: Public Policy Analytics at the University of Pennsylvania.😄
This site documents my work in the Master of Urban Spatial Analytics program — weekly notes, course assignments, and a final project applying data analysis to urban policy questions.



I’m a student in the MUSA program at Penn. My background is in hands-on GIS fieldwork, site analysis, and 3D imagery processing, and I’m interested in smart cities and walkability.

title: About
text: I was born and raised in Hong Kong and moved to the U.S. as a first-generation college student to pursue higher education. I studied Urban Studies and GIS at UC San Diego, where I fell in love with using spatial data to address real-world challenges like walkability, pedestrian safety, and wildfire risk. What drew me to urban spatial analytics is its power to combine data science, mapping, and programming to make cities more equitable, safe, and resilient. Through MUSA, I’m excited to dive into predictive modeling and urban informatics to advance sustainable transportation and hazard mitigation. My goal is to work as a GIS analyst using data to build better urban systems!

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
Most people ignore it. In this assignment, you won’t.
In this analysis, I look at the median age across counties in Florida, and ask which communities we measure most and least reliably.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Choosing what to measure

my_state <- "FL"        # two-letter abbreviation, in quotes
my_variable <- "B01002_001"     # the variable code, in quotes

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Pulling the data

county_data <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = my_variable,
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5"
)

Let’s look at what came back.

dim(county_data)

[1] 67  5

head(county_data)

# A tibble: 6 × 5
  GEOID NAME                     variable   estimate   moe
  <chr> <chr>                    <chr>         <dbl> <dbl>
1 12001 Alachua County, Florida  B01002_001     32.2   0.2
2 12003 Baker County, Florida    B01002_001     38.1   0.7
3 12005 Bay County, Florida      B01002_001     41.4   0.3
4 12007 Bradford County, Florida B01002_001     40.5   1.2
5 12009 Brevard County, Florida  B01002_001     46.8   0.2
6 12011 Broward County, Florida  B01002_001     41.3   0.2


[How many rows did you get? Does that match the number of counties in your state?]
There are 67 counties in Florida and my row count matches.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: How big is the margin of error?
text:
How big is the margin of error?
A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an estimate of 20,000 than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across places, we need it as a percentage.

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)

Now sort to see which counties are measured least reliably.

county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)

# A tibble: 10 × 4
   NAME                      estimate   moe moe_pct
   <chr>                        <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
 1 Lafayette County, Florida     41.8   2.6    6.22
 2 Liberty County, Florida       39.1   2.1    5.37
 3 Glades County, Florida        45.8   1.9    4.15
 4 Gulf County, Florida          47.3   1.5    3.17
 5 Bradford County, Florida      40.5   1.2    2.96
 6 Holmes County, Florida        42.4   1.2    2.83
 7 Jefferson County, Florida     47     1.3    2.77
 8 Calhoun County, Florida       41.8   0.9    2.15
 9 Hamilton County, Florida      40.6   0.8    1.97
10 Gilchrist County, Florida     42.7   0.8    1.87


[Which county has the largest margin of error relative to its estimate? How large is it?]
Lafayette County, Florida has the largest margin of error relative to its estimate, which is around 6.22%.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Sorting counties into reliability categories

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 2  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 5 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

count(county_data, reliability)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  reliability         n
  <chr>           <int>
1 High confidence    59
2 Low confidence      2
3 Moderate            6


[How many counties fall into each category?]
If the cutoff is 5% and 10%, then 65 of them will land to high confidence and only 2 county will land to moderate. That is why I manually change the cutoffs to 2% and 5%, which showcase 59 in high confidence, 6 in moderate and 2 in low confidence.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. That means a wide pull.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                     myvarE myvarM    popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                     <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>
1 12001 Alachua County, Florida    32.2    0.2  281751    NA
2 12003 Baker County, Florida      38.1    0.7   28186    NA
3 12005 Bay County, Florida        41.4    0.3  181368    NA
4 12007 Bradford County, Florida   40.5    1.2   27888    NA
5 12009 Brevard County, Florida    46.8    0.2  620533    NA
6 12011 Broward County, Florida    41.3    0.2 1946127    NA



county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 2  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 5 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

Now compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence         59        369666.
2 Low confidence           2          7842.
3 Moderate                 6         17153.


[What is the average population of high-confidence counties versus low-confidence counties? Is there a pattern?]
The average population of high-confidence counties is 337126 in 65 counties, while the average population of low-confidence is 7842 in 2 counties. It means that larger population sizes have higher data confidence.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
[Your 200–250 word reflection goes here.]

In Florida, the communities we know the least about are small, rural counties such as Lafayette County and Liberty County. In our analysis, Lafayette County had the highest relative margin of error at 6.22%, while Liberty County, Florida have the margin of error at 5.37%. This two counties also fell into the moderate confidence category, with an average population of just 7,842.
This uncertainty stems directly from how the American Community Survey (ACS) operates. Because the ACS collects data from a sample of households rather than conducting a full census count, smaller populations naturally yield smaller sample sizes. With fewer completed responses, individual sample variations will lead to higher random variations on a bigger impact, driving up the margin of error percentage relative to the estimate.
If a state agency allocated funding based on median ages, like distributing senior services grants. Treating every county’s estimate as equally certain means that the rural residents would suffer most. In small counties, less sample calculated median age. If Lafayette County’s median age were underestimated due to sampling error and there is more outliner, state algorithms might misclassify it as a younger community and withhold essential funding for senior centers, elder healthcare, and specialized transit. Meanwhile, large urban counties like Miami-Dade have massive sample sizes, negligible relative error, and stable funding streams. Relying uncritically on ACS estimates without accounting for margin of error disproportionately harms vulnerable, small-town communities by compounding statistical uncertainty with financial deprivation.

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim - Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text: This report checks the claim identified in my draft from Alfred Lubrano’s 2018 WHYY / Philadelphia Inquirer article: Eastwick’s poverty rate rose from 12% in 2006–2010 to 26% in 2013–2017, described as the largest neighborhood increase. This would be a 14-percentage-point increase. Following the assignment, I examine Philadelphia census tracts. The assignment explains that the article does not publish its tract-to-neighborhood groupings, so this analysis can test the broader pattern of change but cannot reproduce Eastwick’s boundaries or ranking.

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim - Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text: This report checks the claim identified in my draft from Alfred Lubrano’s 2018 WHYY / Philadelphia Inquirer article: Eastwick’s poverty rate rose from 12% in 2006–2010 to 26% in 2013–2017, described as the largest neighborhood increase. This would be a 14-percentage-point increase. Following the assignment, I examine Philadelphia census tracts. The assignment explains that the article does not publish its tract-to-neighborhood groupings, so this analysis can test the broader pattern of change but cannot reproduce Eastwick’s boundaries or ranking.

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim - Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text:
Part 1 — Reconstruct
I use B17001_002, the number of people whose income in the past 12 months was below the poverty level, divided by B17001_001, the population for whom poverty status is determined. The denominator is the population covered by this poverty table, rather than the entire population from a separate table. I use the same variables in both periods so that the rates measure the same thing. The Week 3 notes identify B17001_002 as a poverty count; I adapt the practice script’s moe_prop() calculation to this table. The E columns contain estimates and the M columns contain their margins of error.
I request survey = "acs5" with year = 2010 and year = 2017, which represent 2006–2010 and 2013–2017. Five-year estimates are available for tracts, and these are the periods specified in the assignment. The periods do not overlap: they share no survey years. I use the class method that treats their sampling errors as independent. I assume B17001 is an appropriate reconstruction of the article’s poverty measure and that matching tract GEOIDs represent comparable areas. A matching identifier alone does not verify unchanged boundaries. I do not assign neighborhood names to tracts or average tract rates to reconstruct a neighborhood.


Show code
acs_2006_2010 <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  variables = c(

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim - Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text:
Part 2 — Test

Calculate rates and investigate missing values
I combine the two downloads with a period label, then apply the same calculation to every tract-period row. Multiplying both the proportion and its MOE by 100 expresses the rate as a percentage and the MOE in percentage points. I check the original counts before calculating rates: a zero denominator makes a rate undefined, rather than making it a zero-poverty tract. Missing or invalid inputs remain unavailable.


Show code
poverty_rates <- bind_rows(
  acs_2006_2010 %>% mutate(period = "2006-2010"),
  acs_2013_2017 %>% mutate(period = "2013-2017")
) %>%
  mutate(
    input_status = case_when(
      is.na(total_popE) | is.na(total_povertyE) |
        is.na(total_popM) | is.na(total_povertyM) ~ "Missing count or MOE",
      total_popE == 0 ~ "Zero poverty-universe population",
      total_popE < 0 | total_povertyE < 0 |
        total_povertyE > total_popE |
        total_popM < 0 | total_povertyM < 0 ~ "Invalid count or MOE",
      TRUE ~ "Usable"
    ),
    # NA prevents division by zero while preserving the original counts.
    denominator = if_else(input_status == "Usable", total_popE, NA_real_),
    pov_rate = 100 * total_povertyE / denominator,
    pov_rate_moe = 100 * moe_prop(
      total_povertyE, denominator, total_povertyM, total_popM
    ),
    # CV is undefined for a zero rate; its rate and MOE can still be used.
    cv = if_else(pov_rate > 0,
                 (pov_rate_moe / 1.645) / pov_rate * 100, NA_real_),
    reliability = case_when(
      is.na(pov_rate) | is.na(pov_rate_moe) ~ "Unavailable rate or MOE",
      pov_rate == 0 ~ "CV undefined: zero rate",
      cv < 12   ~ "Reliable",
      cv <= 40  ~ "Somewhat reliable",
      TRUE      ~ "Unreliable"
    )
  )

missing_inputs <- poverty_rates %>%
  filter(input_status != "Usable")

missing_inputs %>%
  select(GEOID, period, total_popE, total_povertyE, input_status) %>%
  gt() %>%
  cols_label(
    GEOID = "Tract GEOID", period = "ACS period",
    total_popE = "Total population",
    total_povertyE = "People with poverty", input_status = "Reason"
  ) %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Tract-period inputs that cannot produce a poverty rate",
    subtitle = "Philadelphia | ACS 2006–2010 and 2013–2017"
  )

The input check identifies 15 unusable tract-period rows: 7 in 2006–2010 and 8 in 2013–2017. In these downloads, all have a zero poverty-universe population. This explains their undefined rates; the counts alone do not identify their land use or prove that their total resident population is zero. I retain these rows in the audit and exclude a tract from the change test if either period lacks a usable rate or MOE.


Match tracts and test changes
I join by GEOID, following the Week 4 notes. A full join keeps unmatched identifiers visible. Change is the later rate minus the earlier rate, in percentage points. Following the practice script, I divide each MOE by 1.645 to get its standard error, combine the two standard errors, and multiply by 1.645 for the MOE of the change. A change is detectable at 90% confidence when abs(z) > 1.645, meaning its interval excludes zero. Reliability describes the precision of an individual rate; it is separate from this test of change.


Show code
selected_2010 <- poverty_rates %>%
  filter(period == "2006-2010") %>%
  select(GEOID, pov_rate_2010 = pov_rate, pov_moe_2010 = pov_rate_moe)

selected_2017 <- poverty_rates %>%
  filter(period == "2013-2017") %>%
  select(GEOID, pov_rate_2017 = pov_rate, pov_moe_2017 = pov_rate_moe)

unmatched_2010 <- anti_join(selected_2010, selected_2017, by = "GEOID")
unmatched_2017 <- anti_join(selected_2017, selected_2010, by = "GEOID")

poverty_wide <- full_join(selected_2010, selected_2017, by = "GEOID")

poverty_tested <- poverty_wide %>%
  mutate(
    change = pov_rate_2017 - pov_rate_2010,
    se_1 = pov_moe_2010 / 1.645,
    se_2 = pov_moe_2017 / 1.645,
    se_diff = sqrt(se_1^2 + se_2^2),
    moe_diff = se_diff * 1.645,
    z = if_else(se_diff > 0, change / se_diff, NA_real_),
    significant = abs(z) > 1.645,
    result = case_when(
      is.na(significant) ~ "Not testable",
      significant & change > 0 ~ "Detectable increase",
      significant & change < 0 ~ "Detectable decrease",
      TRUE ~ "No detectable change"
    )
  )


# Create the summary before the inline R expressions use it below.
test_summary <- poverty_tested %>%
  summarize(
    total = n(),
    tested = sum(!is.na(significant)),
    detected = sum(significant, na.rm = TRUE),
    not_detected = sum(!significant, na.rm = TRUE),
    excluded = sum(is.na(significant)),
    increases = sum(result == "Detectable increase"),
    decreases = sum(result == "Detectable decrease"),
    apparent_increases = sum(change > 0, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

change_counts <- poverty_tested %>% count(result, name = "tracts")
change_counts %>%
  gt() %>%
  cols_label(result = "90% change-test result", tracts = "Number of tracts") %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Poverty-rate change across Philadelphia tracts",
    subtitle = "ACS 2013–2017 minus 2006–2010 | All downloaded GEOIDs"
  )

Show change and its uncertainty

  filter(!is.na(significant)) %>%
  arrange(GEOID) %>%
  slice_head(n = 15)

ggplot(plot_tracts, aes(x = reorder(GEOID, change), y = change)) +
  geom_col(aes(fill = result)) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(ymin = change - moe_diff, ymax = change + moe_diff),
    width = 0.3
  ) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Poverty-rate changes in 15 Philadelphia tracts",
    subtitle = "ACS 2013–2017 minus 2006–2010 | Error bars show 90% MOEs",
    x = "Tract GEOID", y = "Change in poverty rate (percentage points)",
    fill = "90% test", caption = "Source: ACS B17001 via tidycensus"
  )








Figure 1: Estimated changes and 90% margins of error for the first 15 testable tract GEOIDs in ascending order. This is an illustrative subset, not a neighborhood grouping or a ranking of changes.





The dashed line marks zero change. An error bar crossing this line means that the estimated change is not statistically detectable. Bars above zero are estimated increases; those below zero are estimated decreases. The chart keeps both detectable and non-detectable changes so the reader can compare them.


Reliability of the rates
The CV is the rate’s standard error divided by its estimate, multiplied by 100. I use the assignment’s thresholds: below 12% reliable, 12–40% somewhat reliable, and above 40% unreliable. Exactly 40% is therefore somewhat reliable. The symbols below provide the required coding without relying on color alone. The table highlights the 15 tract-period estimates with the highest defined CVs; it is not a summary of the typical tract.


Show code
poverty_rates %>%
  filter(!is.na(cv)) %>%
  arrange(desc(cv)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 15) %>%
  select(GEOID, period, pov_rate, pov_rate_moe, cv, reliability) %>%
  gt() %>%
  fmt_number(columns = c(pov_rate, pov_rate_moe, cv), decimals = 1) %>%
  cols_label(
    GEOID = "Tract GEOID", period = "ACS period",
    pov_rate = "Poverty rate (%)", pov_rate_moe = "90% MOE (pp)",
    cv = "CV (%)", reliability = "Reliability"
  ) %>%
  cols_align(align = "center") %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Philadelphia poverty rates with the highest relative uncertainty",
    subtitle = "15 tract-period estimates | ACS 2006–2010 and 2013–2017"
  )

Some margins of error are large relative to the rate itself. I retain uncertain but calculable estimates in the change test because removing them would hide part of the evidence. A large MOE widens the change interval and makes a detectable result harder to establish.


Put the illustrated changes in context


Show code

  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_text(aes(label = tracts), hjust = -0.15) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  coord_flip() +

    title = "Most tract changes are not statistically detectable",

  )

The full count provides context for the small error-bar sample. There are 211 positive point-estimate changes, but only 36 detectable increases. Looking only at the signs of the changes would overstate the evidence for rising poverty.

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim - Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text:
Part 3 — Adjudicate
Supported: the broader idea that poverty rates increased in some Philadelphia areas is consistent with the tract evidence: 36 tracts have detectable increases. Change is not uniform, however; 27 tracts have detectable decreases. Not supported: interpreting every positive estimate as established worsening would go beyond the evidence. Of 211 positive changes, only 36 pass the 90% test, and 313 testable tracts overall have intervals that include zero. This is a limit on what can be inferred from the estimates, not evidence that the article explicitly claimed every tract worsened or that every non-detectable change is actually zero.
Cannot be determined: the specific claim that Eastwick rose from 12% to 26%, and especially that its increase was the largest among neighborhoods, cannot be established or contradicted by these tract results. The assignment says the article’s neighborhood groupings are unavailable. A neighborhood rate would require the appropriate aggregated counts and their uncertainty, not an average of tract percentages. A tract with an increase above 14 percentage points would not disprove Eastwick’s neighborhood ranking because tracts and neighborhoods are different units. This report also makes no finding about the article title’s racial comparisons: the two variables used here describe poverty for the full poverty universe, without a race breakdown.

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim - Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text:
Part 4 — Rewrite
Philadelphia’s poverty changes were uneven between 2006–2010 and 2013–2017. Among 376 census tracts with usable estimates, 36 showed a statistically detectable increase in poverty rates and 27 showed a detectable decrease at 90% confidence. Changes in the other 313 tracts were too uncertain to distinguish from zero. Another 8 tracts could not be compared because their poverty rates were undefined in at least one period. These findings support increases in some parts of the city, but they do not establish Eastwick’s reported rise from 12% to 26% or its ranking among neighborhoods. Checking those claims requires the tract groupings used to define each neighborhood.
